extracted.intended_audience: legal scholars, judges, administrative law practitioners, and law students interested in the Administrative Procedure Act and notice-and-comment rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Critical analysis of legal norms and interpretive criteria governing notice-and-comment rulemaking and judicial review under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), including debates over originalism, deference, hard-look review, and the major questions doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice-and-comment rulemaking (public notice and participation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The APA’s big policy innovation is notice-and-comment rulemaking, which asserted the kind of due process that agencies were to provide: agencies must provide public notice and receive and consider public comments, acting transparently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion requires that agencies make rules through an open process—giving notice of proposed rules, soliciting public comment, and creating a public record. The article treats notice-and-comment as the principal mechanism by which agencies supply democratic legitimacy and due process when engaging in large-scale lawmaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsiveness to public comments (respond to the most serious ones)
rubrics_metrics.description: To give efficacy to the APA’s requirement that rules not be arbitrary or capricious, the agency must pay attention to the public comments and must respond to the most serious ones with reasoning tied to the statutory purposes and plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must explain why they accept or reject comments and alternatives; courts have faulted agencies for not addressing 'alternative way[s] of achieving the objectives of the Act' (citing Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass’n v. State Farm). Failure to engage materially with substantive comments risks arbitrary-and-capricious review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive reason-giving and public justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency decisions were to be substantively reasonable, publicly justified, and responsive to public comments; agencies must give reasons for their actions that are tied to the proceedings leading to the decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason-giving is owed to the electorate (via accountability) and to courts and Congress; justifications should be grounded in law and fact and should allow meaningful judicial review rather than being mere policy pronouncements or secret rationales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of judicial review (availability of review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial review of final agency rulemaking is presumptively available under the APA, with exceptions disfavored (see 5 U.S.C. § 702).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article treats the presumption of review as an essential part of the APA’s deep compromise—courts generally should be available to police arbitrary or unlawful agency action unless a clear exception applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hard-look (arbitrariness) review of agency factual conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: The APA encourages a hard look at fishy agency reasoning; courts should examine agency factual conclusions with searching review to ensure they are not arbitrary or capricious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hard-look review requires courts to ensure agencies have considered the relevant factors, explained the basis for their factual findings, and addressed important counterarguments and alternatives. The doctrine functions as a check on agency discretion within the APA framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to explain rejection of reasonable alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must explain why they reject reasonable alternatives in rulemaking and how their final rules accord with statutory purpose as applied to facts on the ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to demonstrate consideration of reasonable alternatives or to tie choices to statutory objectives invites reversal under arbitrary-and-capricious standards; Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass’n v. State Farm is invoked as the exemplar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deference to agency interpretations (sympathetic, informed judicial reading)
rubrics_metrics.description: The APA supports deferential consideration of agency interpretations of law under many circumstances; judges should assume responsibility but read statutory text sympathetically, informed by legislative deliberations, agencies’ fact-based understanding, and private/public reliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article roots deference in the APA’s deep compromise and cites leading cases (Skidmore, Seminole Rock/Bowles, Hearst) as consistent with the APA. Deference is contextual and justified where agencies possess expertise and have engaged in reasoned decisionmaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to expansion of the major questions doctrine (avoid antideference for large-impact rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Roberts Court’s creation of a 'major questions doctrine' that antidefers to agency rulemaking having large social or economic effects is criticized as inconsistent with the APA’s deep compromise and as an illegitimate judicial substitution for democratic processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article argues that super-strong clear-statement rules and triply undemocratic applications of the major questions doctrine (undemocratic court majority, trumping accountable agency deliberation, imposing a clarity tax on Congress) undermine democratic legitimacy and effective agency governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy standard for administrative common law (democratic pedigree via institutional interaction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative common law is legitimate when it secures a 'democratic pedigree' through challenge-and-response among lower courts, agencies, DOJ, the White House, Congress, and the regulated community; such institutional interaction constitutes public dialogue that can entrench norms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where judicially developed doctrines emerge from sustained institutional interaction and public contestation rather than unilateral judicial fiat, they better reflect the APA’s role as a super-statute and are more democratically defensible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive method for super-statutes (deep compromise / intensional approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: For super-statutes like the APA, original public meaning should focus on the law’s important concepts and purposes (a 'deep compromise') rather than an extensional, time-machine approach that freezes detailed compromises; prefer an intensional approach to historical meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This interpretive criterion counsels that courts and scholars should discern the foundational concepts (balance between democratic accountability and administrative competence) underpinning the APA, allowing the statute to be responsibly applied to novel modern problems rather than rigidly tethered to 1946 specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency accountability akin to legislative justification
rubrics_metrics.description: When agencies make legally binding rules, they should, as far as possible, do so in the same ways that Congress would—give reasons and justifications for action that can be examined by elected officials and the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This demands transparency, public recordkeeping, and reasoned explanations so that agencies are accountable both politically (through Congress and elections) and legally (through judicial review).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject substitution of a 'juriscentric' regulatory vision
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts should avoid substituting a juriscentric vision for the regulatory state—i.e., courts should not replace agency policy implementation faithfully tied to congressional policies with their own regulatory judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This standard admonishes judges to respect the institutional roles allocated by the APA’s deep compromise: agencies implement and interpret policy within delegated authority, while courts ensure legality and reasoned process rather than supplanting policy choices.
